1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
4	Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
5	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
6	Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
7	Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
8	This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.
9	
10	\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
11	All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
12	Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
13	The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
14	For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
15	Cross-architecture validation across 14 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 12 of 14 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
16	$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions (11/14 pending Padding-410M audit), confirming that multi-method agreement generalizes beyond the calibration setup; Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8) reflect scale-dependent seed sensitivity and canary metric splitting rather than framework failure.
17	Reverse-direction tests at $\alpha{=}1.0$ reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence at full synthetic replacement), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
18	The unidirectionality of token entropy is domain-dependent: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4 (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling absent from all WikiText conditions at any contamination level (see below).
19	GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
20	Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
21	Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
22	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance, placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
23	The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
24	Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
25	The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
26	Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (consistent with the null regime) and moderate detection (3--4/8) only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
27	
28	\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to method recommendation.}
29	The primary value of the multi-method framework is not the consensus vote itself but the systematic comparison it enables.
30	By applying five methods with different inductive biases to the same data, the framework reveals \emph{why} each method succeeds or fails: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR because it captures reverse-directional associations; differenced cross-correlation cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence; threshold onset lacks power at $T{=}11$ under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}); and Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8) but remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
31	This process of elimination converges on permutation Granger as the recommended method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation on WikiText (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
32	The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution, maintaining FPR${=}$0\%; however, the practical recommendation is simpler: for short iterative training series, permutation Granger alone provides reliable detection without requiring the full consensus machinery.
33	Multi-method consensus ($K{\geq}3$) remains useful as a robustness check, reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 cross-architecture conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), but threshold onset is power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with four contributing methods supporting the $K{\geq}3$ threshold.
34	
35	\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
36	With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
37	This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
38	After correcting a statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), confirming that its lower rates reflect genuine power limitations at $T{=}11$ rather than implementation error.
39	This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
40	Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
41	However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
42	After implementation correction, Toda--Yamamoto's window sensitivity is consistent with its moderate detection profile: TY consensus stabilizes at $T{\geq}6$, slightly later than the primary methods ($T{\geq}5$), reflecting the additional degrees of freedom consumed by the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
43	
44	\paragraph{Four-layer detection taxonomy.}
45	Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
46	(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$ (established);
47	(2)~\emph{Distributional instability} (entropy variance): detects inflated fluctuations in canary metrics across generations, with suggestive onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$ (a $10\times$ variance inflation from $0.004$ to $0.04$), well before causal coupling emerges;
48	(3)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
49	(4)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (AC1): suggestive evidence of autocorrelation shifts near the onset boundary (see below), but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$.
50	Layers~1 and~3 are established; Layers~2 and~4 are suggestive and require longer generation protocols for confirmation ($T{\geq}50$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}).
51	These four layers are complementary rather than redundant: dimensionality collapse and distributional instability precede causal detectability by a wide margin, and the layers can diverge across architectures.
52	
53	\paragraph{Suggestive CSD signatures at the onset boundary.}
54	Exploratory analysis of classical critical slowing down indicators reveals patterns consistent with---but not confirmatory of---CSD predictions at the detection phase transition.
55	Token entropy AC1 exhibits a $+0.30$ jump at the onset boundary (from $-0.58$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ to $-0.28$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$); although AC1 remains negative throughout, the direction of the jump aligns with the CSD prediction that autocorrelation increases near critical transitions~\cite{scheffer2009early}.
56	Token entropy variance undergoes a $10\times$ inflation at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($0.004 \to 0.04$), far earlier than the PermG onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$, suggesting that distributional instability precedes causal detectability---consistent with Layer~2 of the taxonomy above.
57	The anomalously negative AC1 at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($-0.58$) may reflect critical speeding-up~\cite{titus2020speeding}, where indicators exhibit non-monotonic behavior immediately before a transition.
58	These patterns are suggestive but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$, where the 95\% confidence interval for AC1 is approximately $\pm 0.3$; longer generation protocols ($T{\geq}50$--$100$) would be needed for formal CSD testing~\cite{dakos2012methods}.
59	
60	\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
61	As a distributional dimensionality indicator, effective rank tracks contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---Layer~1 in the taxonomy above.
62	However, effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
63	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
64	In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
65	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
66	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.
67	
68	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
69	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
70	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
71	This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.
72	
73	\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
74	The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the $S \times R$ prediction in \S\ref{sec:theory}: at $\alpha{=}0.60$, relaxation time matching drives temporal resolution $R \to 0$---entropy and diversity respond within the same generation---so that despite increasing signal strength $S$, the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
75	At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $R$ remains high---entropy leads diversity by a full generation---and $S$ has just crossed the detection threshold, yielding sufficient $S \times R$.
76	At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), $S$ grows large enough to dominate: entropy collapses within generation~0$\to$1 while diversity still requires generation~1$\to$2, restoring $R$ and driving $S \times R$ well above the detection floor.
77	The synchronous dip is mechanistically distinct from the blind regime: in the blind regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous dip, both metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
78	This creates a four-regime structure---blind, onset, synchronous dip, detection---rather than the two-regime detect/no-detect boundary assumed by simpler models.
79	Toda--Yamamoto maintains moderate detection (3--4/8) across the $\alpha{=}0.50$--$0.75$ range including the synchronous zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8, suggesting partial inter-method complementarity: TY's augmented VAR formulation may be less sensitive to the temporal synchronization that suppresses PermG's signal at $\alpha{=}0.60$.
80	The finding also has practical implications: simple threshold-based triggers (e.g., the 15\% entropy criterion) fire at $\alpha{=}0.60$ because they respond to magnitude rather than temporal structure, suggesting that threshold triggers may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.
81	
82	\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
83	The unidirectional forward causation observed consistently in WikiText experiments (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all contamination levels and seeds) does not hold universally.
84	On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Pythia-410M, s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8 (forward: 8/8), indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling between canary and downstream metrics (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
85	This stands in sharp contrast to the same model at the same contamination level on WikiText, where PermG reverse${=}$0/8.
86	One possible explanation is that C4's broader distributional characteristics (Common Crawl vs.\ encyclopedic Wikipedia text) alter the temporal dynamics of collapse: the richer distributional structure may allow downstream diversity metrics to feed back into canary metrics more quickly, shortening the temporal offset that WikiText's narrower distribution preserves.
87	Alternatively, the pre-training data confound (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) may play a role, since Pythia was pre-trained on the Pile which includes C4-overlapping data.
88	The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain rather than assumed to transfer from WikiText-based calibration; the forward detection itself (PermG fwd${=}$8/8) remains robust across both domains.
89	
90	\paragraph{Canary metric choice as a sensitivity dimension.}
91	SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a dimension of method sensitivity beyond the five statistical methods analyzed in Claim~3.
92	Token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations in SmolLM3, violating the monotonic decline assumed by Granger tests and producing 0/4 significant entropy$\to$downstream pairs.
93	ECE, by contrast, maintains monotonic growth and achieves 3/4 significant pairs (PermG fwd: 3/8 overall).
94	The two canary types activate through partially disjoint method subsets: entropy pairs reach significance via naive and differenced cross-correlation, while ECE pairs reach significance via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger.
95	SmolLM3-3B achieves $K{\geq}3$ = 3/8 (matching PermG fwd), confirming that consensus tracks individual-method detection even in this challenging case; however, the low overall detection (3/8) places SmolLM3 as one of three outliers ($K{\geq}3$ $<6/8$) across the 14-condition cross-architecture panel.
96	This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal.
97	The practical implication is that monitoring dashboards should track multiple canary candidates, adapting the active metric to the architecture under evaluation.
98	
99	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
100	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
101	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
102	At $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, where early warning would be most valuable, aggregate canary detection remains null (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ but does not reach aggregate detection through $\alpha{=}0.45$).
103	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
104	This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
105	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
106	This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
107	At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
108	This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
109	The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
110	If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.
111	
112	\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
113	In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
114	A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
115	The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
116	The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.
117	
118	\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
119	Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
120	This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
121	Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, provide cross-scale evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
122	Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
123	Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
124	These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
125	The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.
126	
127	\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
128	In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
129	Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
130	The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
131	The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the scope of intervention validation (three seed-precision pairs across two model scales at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment---particularly to larger models and accumulate-mode training---requires further confirmation.
132	The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; notably, the threshold trigger fires at $\alpha{=}0.60$ even though formal Granger detection fails at this level (synchronous collapse zone; \S\ref{sec:regime}), illustrating that magnitude-based triggers can complement temporal-precedence tests.
133	However, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.
134	
135	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
136	The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
137	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
138	The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
139	In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
140	First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
141	Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.
142	
143	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
144	Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
145	First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
146	This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods; Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection (3--4/8) at $T{=}11$ reflects this constraint, as the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ consumes additional degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
147	Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
148	Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
149	Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
150	These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.
151	
152	\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
153	We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
154	TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
155	This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
156	The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
157	This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.
158	
159	Change-point analysis under the null condition ($\alpha{=}0.00$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
160	Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary$\to$downstream significance (24/24) while eliminating reverse-direction signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).
161	
162	\paragraph{Future work.}
163	Several directions extend this work.
164	Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
165	Multi-seed replication across the six validated architecture families would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}7$B parameters) remains an open direction.
166	Longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$ generations) could unlock threshold onset detection, which requires more generation-over-generation differences for $3\sigma$ calibration to achieve adequate power; longer runs could also improve Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection rates by providing additional degrees of freedom for the augmented VAR (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
167	The SmolLM3 finding (ECE-only detection due to non-monotonic entropy) motivates systematic study of which canary metric is most reliable per architecture family.
168	Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
169	Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
170	The sigmoid quantification of the onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) invites connection to theoretical frameworks---the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr} and the universality classes of \citet{truong2025entropy}---that could explain why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime and whether the non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reflects a transition boundary; these connections remain speculative and require finer $\alpha$ resolution to validate.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
Cross-architecture validation across 14 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 12 of 14 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions (11/14 pending Padding-410M audit), confirming that multi-method agreement generalizes beyond the calibration setup; Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8) reflect scale-dependent seed sensitivity and canary metric splitting rather than framework failure.
Reverse-direction tests at $\alpha{=}1.0$ reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence at full synthetic replacement), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
The unidirectionality of token entropy is domain-dependent: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4 (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling absent from all WikiText conditions at any contamination level (see below).
GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance, placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (consistent with the null regime) and moderate detection (3--4/8) only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to method recommendation.}
The primary value of the multi-method framework is not the consensus vote itself but the systematic comparison it enables.
By applying five methods with different inductive biases to the same data, the framework reveals \emph{why} each method succeeds or fails: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR because it captures reverse-directional associations; differenced cross-correlation cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence; threshold onset lacks power at $T{=}11$ under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}); and Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8) but remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
This process of elimination converges on permutation Granger as the recommended method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation on WikiText (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution, maintaining FPR${=}$0\%; however, the practical recommendation is simpler: for short iterative training series, permutation Granger alone provides reliable detection without requiring the full consensus machinery.
Multi-method consensus ($K{\geq}3$) remains useful as a robustness check, reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 cross-architecture conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), but threshold onset is power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with four contributing methods supporting the $K{\geq}3$ threshold.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
After correcting a statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), confirming that its lower rates reflect genuine power limitations at $T{=}11$ rather than implementation error.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
After implementation correction, Toda--Yamamoto's window sensitivity is consistent with its moderate detection profile: TY consensus stabilizes at $T{\geq}6$, slightly later than the primary methods ($T{\geq}5$), reflecting the additional degrees of freedom consumed by the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{Four-layer detection taxonomy.}
Our results suggest a layered taxonomy for detecting iterative training degradation, ordered by onset threshold:
(1)~\emph{Distributional dimensionality} (effective rank): detects contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom, with onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.10$ (established);
(2)~\emph{Distributional instability} (entropy variance): detects inflated fluctuations in canary metrics across generations, with suggestive onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$ (a $10\times$ variance inflation from $0.004$ to $0.04$), well before causal coupling emerges;
(3)~\emph{Causal coupling} (Granger-type tests): detects temporal precedence between canary and downstream metrics, with onset at $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$ (the detection phase transition established in \S\ref{sec:regime}); and
(4)~\emph{Dynamical stability} (AC1): suggestive evidence of autocorrelation shifts near the onset boundary (see below), but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$.
Layers~1 and~3 are established; Layers~2 and~4 are suggestive and require longer generation protocols for confirmation ($T{\geq}50$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}).
These four layers are complementary rather than redundant: dimensionality collapse and distributional instability precede causal detectability by a wide margin, and the layers can diverge across architectures.

\paragraph{Suggestive CSD signatures at the onset boundary.}
Exploratory analysis of classical critical slowing down indicators reveals patterns consistent with---but not confirmatory of---CSD predictions at the detection phase transition.
Token entropy AC1 exhibits a $+0.30$ jump at the onset boundary (from $-0.58$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ to $-0.28$ at $\alpha{=}0.50$); although AC1 remains negative throughout, the direction of the jump aligns with the CSD prediction that autocorrelation increases near critical transitions~\cite{scheffer2009early}.
Token entropy variance undergoes a $10\times$ inflation at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($0.004 \to 0.04$), far earlier than the PermG onset at $\alpha{\approx}0.50$, suggesting that distributional instability precedes causal detectability---consistent with Layer~2 of the taxonomy above.
The anomalously negative AC1 at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($-0.58$) may reflect critical speeding-up~\cite{titus2020speeding}, where indicators exhibit non-monotonic behavior immediately before a transition.
These patterns are suggestive but not statistically conclusive at $T{=}11$, where the 95\% confidence interval for AC1 is approximately $\pm 0.3$; longer generation protocols ($T{\geq}50$--$100$) would be needed for formal CSD testing~\cite{dakos2012methods}.

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
As a distributional dimensionality indicator, effective rank tracks contraction of the distribution's effective degrees of freedom---Layer~1 in the taxonomy above.
However, effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines---a limitation specific to the dimensionality layer that does not affect the causal coupling layer (Granger detectability), which remains consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) is consistent with the $S \times R$ prediction in \S\ref{sec:theory}: at $\alpha{=}0.60$, relaxation time matching drives temporal resolution $R \to 0$---entropy and diversity respond within the same generation---so that despite increasing signal strength $S$, the product $S \times R$ reaches a local minimum.
At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $R$ remains high---entropy leads diversity by a full generation---and $S$ has just crossed the detection threshold, yielding sufficient $S \times R$.
At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), $S$ grows large enough to dominate: entropy collapses within generation~0$\to$1 while diversity still requires generation~1$\to$2, restoring $R$ and driving $S \times R$ well above the detection floor.
The synchronous dip is mechanistically distinct from the blind regime: in the blind regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous dip, both metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
This creates a four-regime structure---blind, onset, synchronous dip, detection---rather than the two-regime detect/no-detect boundary assumed by simpler models.
Toda--Yamamoto maintains moderate detection (3--4/8) across the $\alpha{=}0.50$--$0.75$ range including the synchronous zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8, suggesting partial inter-method complementarity: TY's augmented VAR formulation may be less sensitive to the temporal synchronization that suppresses PermG's signal at $\alpha{=}0.60$.
The finding also has practical implications: simple threshold-based triggers (e.g., the 15\% entropy criterion) fire at $\alpha{=}0.60$ because they respond to magnitude rather than temporal structure, suggesting that threshold triggers may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
The unidirectional forward causation observed consistently in WikiText experiments (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all contamination levels and seeds) does not hold universally.
On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Pythia-410M, s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8 (forward: 8/8), indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling between canary and downstream metrics (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
This stands in sharp contrast to the same model at the same contamination level on WikiText, where PermG reverse${=}$0/8.
One possible explanation is that C4's broader distributional characteristics (Common Crawl vs.\ encyclopedic Wikipedia text) alter the temporal dynamics of collapse: the richer distributional structure may allow downstream diversity metrics to feed back into canary metrics more quickly, shortening the temporal offset that WikiText's narrower distribution preserves.
Alternatively, the pre-training data confound (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) may play a role, since Pythia was pre-trained on the Pile which includes C4-overlapping data.
The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain rather than assumed to transfer from WikiText-based calibration; the forward detection itself (PermG fwd${=}$8/8) remains robust across both domains.

\paragraph{Canary metric choice as a sensitivity dimension.}
SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a dimension of method sensitivity beyond the five statistical methods analyzed in Claim~3.
Token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations in SmolLM3, violating the monotonic decline assumed by Granger tests and producing 0/4 significant entropy$\to$downstream pairs.
ECE, by contrast, maintains monotonic growth and achieves 3/4 significant pairs (PermG fwd: 3/8 overall).
The two canary types activate through partially disjoint method subsets: entropy pairs reach significance via naive and differenced cross-correlation, while ECE pairs reach significance via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger.
SmolLM3-3B achieves $K{\geq}3$ = 3/8 (matching PermG fwd), confirming that consensus tracks individual-method detection even in this challenging case; however, the low overall detection (3/8) places SmolLM3 as one of three outliers ($K{\geq}3$ $<6/8$) across the 14-condition cross-architecture panel.
This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal.
The practical implication is that monitoring dashboards should track multiple canary candidates, adapting the active metric to the architecture under evaluation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, where early warning would be most valuable, aggregate canary detection remains null (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ but does not reach aggregate detection through $\alpha{=}0.45$).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, provide cross-scale evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the scope of intervention validation (three seed-precision pairs across two model scales at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment---particularly to larger models and accumulate-mode training---requires further confirmation.
The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; notably, the threshold trigger fires at $\alpha{=}0.60$ even though formal Granger detection fails at this level (synchronous collapse zone; \S\ref{sec:regime}), illustrating that magnitude-based triggers can complement temporal-precedence tests.
However, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods; Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection (3--4/8) at $T{=}11$ reflects this constraint, as the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ consumes additional degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.

Change-point analysis under the null condition ($\alpha{=}0.00$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary$\to$downstream significance (24/24) while eliminating reverse-direction signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the six validated architecture families would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}7$B parameters) remains an open direction.
Longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$ generations) could unlock threshold onset detection, which requires more generation-over-generation differences for $3\sigma$ calibration to achieve adequate power; longer runs could also improve Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection rates by providing additional degrees of freedom for the augmented VAR (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
The SmolLM3 finding (ECE-only detection due to non-monotonic entropy) motivates systematic study of which canary metric is most reliable per architecture family.
Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
The sigmoid quantification of the onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) invites connection to theoretical frameworks---the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr} and the universality classes of \citet{truong2025entropy}---that could explain why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime and whether the non-monotonic dip at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reflects a transition boundary; these connections remain speculative and require finer $\alpha$ resolution to validate.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model collapse in iterative training.}

The phenomenon of iterative training collapse was formalized by \citet{shumailov2024curse}, who showed that recursively replacing real data with model-generated text causes progressive tail erosion across VAEs, GMMs, and language models, and by \citet{alemohammad2024mad}, who demonstrated quality--diversity tradeoffs in self-consuming generative loops for image models.
Theoretical analyses have since sharpened these results: \citet{dohmatob2024tale} recast collapse as a change in scaling-law exponents, showing that even small fractions of synthetic data alter effective scaling behavior, while \citet{dohmatob2025strong} proved that collapse can occur even when synthetic data constitutes a vanishingly small fraction of the training set.
\citet{hataya2023will} provided early empirical evidence that large-scale generative models degrade future datasets through web-scale contamination, showing that even state-of-the-art models produce training-data artifacts detectable in downstream models, a finding that motivates our focus on contamination-level-dependent analysis.
\citet{seddik2024bad} formalized the statistical analysis of training on synthetic data, deriving excess risk bounds that quantify how synthetic fraction and model misspecification jointly govern degradation; their framework predicts regime-dependent behavior consistent with the onset boundary we observe empirically at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$.
The role of data accumulation has been a central theme.
\citet{dey2024breaking} proved that accumulating data across generations (rather than replacing it) prevents divergence of population risk in GMMs, HMMs, and language models.
\citet{kazdan2025collapse} systematically compared replace and accumulate regimes, finding that synthetic data value depends on the absolute quantity of co-present real data.
\citet{fu2025selfconsuming} provided generalization bounds for self-consuming loops, establishing that a constant fraction of real data suffices for convergence under accumulation.
On the calibration side, \citet{he2025golden} showed that optimal real-data weighting converges to the golden-ratio inverse ($1/\varphi \approx 0.618$) in Gaussian and GLM settings, and that the risk landscape is non-monotone in mixing ratio, a theoretical prediction with implications for regime-dependent canary behavior.
Beyond distributional statistics, \citet{guo2024linguistic} documented progressive decline in lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across iterative fine-tuning generations, providing the multi-level diversity metrics that serve as downstream targets in our lead-lag analysis.
\citet{schaeffer2025position} catalogued eight distinct and sometimes contradictory definitions of ``model collapse'' in the literature, underscoring the importance of explicit operational definitions, a concern our framework addresses by scoping canary prediction to diversity metrics specifically.

\paragraph{Canary metrics and collapse monitoring.}

Several recent works have proposed monitoring metrics that precede or accompany distributional degradation during iterative training.
\citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models, interpreting this through a geometric-regulation lens.
\citet{du2025scales} report a similar pattern across model scales and mixing ratios, noting that ECE increases of 75\% appear at 30\% synthetic contamination before accuracy drops become visible.
Beyond calibration, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} introduces a dual-track spectral framework based on embedding Gram matrices, where divergence between deterministic and stochastic spectral bounds serves as an early collapse diagnostic.
\citet{kalinowski2026topology} proposes a topological monitoring approach using persistent homology features to detect multi-scale structural loss in representation space.
DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal and reports improvements in ECE and entropy preservation.
\citet{gambetta2024surplexity} introduces surplexity, a surprise-based metric that simultaneously detects collapse and filters training data, demonstrating that high-surplexity selection matches human-data baselines in maintaining distributional balance.

These works collectively demonstrate growing interest in collapse monitoring, yet they share methodological limitations that weaken their lead-lag claims.
None apply differencing tests to distinguish genuine temporal precedence from spurious co-trending; none cross-validate findings across multiple statistical methods; and none apply false discovery rate correction when testing multiple metric pairs.
Our work differs from the closest predecessor, \citet{du2026geometric}, in four respects:
(i)~we compare an entire family of canary metrics rather than a single metric pair;
(ii)~we cross-validate each lead-lag relationship across five independent statistical methods, quantifying inter-method sensitivity via Cohen's $\kappa$ and intra-method sensitivity via augmentation order $d_{\max}$;
(iii)~we map detectability as a function of contamination regime rather than reporting a single aggregate result; and
(iv)~we treat method-selection sensitivity itself as a primary finding, showing that it is the dominant source of variation in existing lead-lag conclusions.

\paragraph{Training dynamics monitoring.}

A broader literature tracks within-training diagnostics such as loss of plasticity~\cite{dohare2024plasticity,lyle2023plasticity}, effective representation rank, and gradient norm statistics as indicators of learning health.
These approaches monitor a single training run and detect pathologies (saturated units, rank collapse, unstable gradients) that emerge over optimization steps.
Our work differs in a key structural way: we analyze \emph{cross-generation} temporal relationships between aggregate statistics computed after each full training cycle, applying time-series causal methods to a sequence of $T{=}10$ generation-level observations rather than tracking step-level dynamics within a single run.
This distinction is methodologically consequential because the short, non-stationary series that arise from generational measurement require entirely different statistical tools (Granger causality, permutation tests, differencing diagnostics) than the long, dense traces available from step-level monitoring.

\paragraph{Early-warning signals and critical transitions.}

The theoretical foundation for canary-based prediction of system failure originates in ecology and climate science.
\citet{scheffer2009early} established that complex systems approaching tipping points exhibit generic early-warning signals (rising autocorrelation and variance due to critical slowing down), independent of system-specific mechanisms.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} extended this framework by combining empirical warning indicators with network-architecture analysis, arguing that structural and statistical signals together improve anticipatory power.
Crucially, \citet{boettiger2012limits} quantified the statistical detection limits of these signals, showing that early-warning power is often negligible in short time series, a constraint directly relevant to iterative training, where the number of generations (typically 5--20) is far smaller than typical ecological datasets.
\citet{truong2025entropy} connects entropy collapse to critical transitions, characterizing it as a first-order phase transition with universality classes that determine whether classical early-warning signals retain predictive power.
\citet{gu2024cmr} establish a scaling law for predicting critical mixture ratios in continual pre-training, demonstrating that the boundary between beneficial and harmful data mixing follows a power-law relationship with training scale, suggesting that onset boundaries in collapse monitoring may have principled theoretical explanations.
The model collapse literature has not yet imported these methodological tools: existing canary studies neither frame their claims in terms of detection power under finite samples nor test whether observed lead-lag patterns survive the short-series constraints that \citet{boettiger2012limits} identified as fundamental.

\paragraph{Lead-lag methodology.}

Granger causality~\cite{granger1969investigating} provides the standard econometric framework for testing whether one time series improves prediction of another beyond its own history.
\citet{shojaie2022granger} review classical and modern extensions, including VAR-based tests, kernel methods, and neural approaches for nonlinear dependencies \cite{marcinkevics2022neural}.
A key practical issue is non-stationarity: standard Granger tests applied to integrated (unit-root) series produce inflated rejection rates, the spurious regression problem formalized by \citet{granger1974spurious}, who demonstrated that regressions between independent random walks yield spuriously significant $t$-statistics, a hazard directly applicable to co-trending metrics in iterative training.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical} addresses this by augmenting the VAR lag order by the integration order $d_{\max}$ and testing only the original lags, yielding valid asymptotic inference regardless of cointegration structure; however, this robustness comes at the cost of reduced degrees of freedom, a trade-off that becomes severe in the short series ($T{\leq}20$) typical of iterative training studies.
Despite wide use in economics and neuroscience, these methods are largely absent from the machine learning literature on iterative training.
Existing canary studies rely on visual inspection or naive cross-correlation, which cannot distinguish genuine temporal precedence from shared non-stationary trends.
Our framework applies five complementary methods (naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset detection, permutation Granger causality, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality) and requires multi-method consensus before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust, directly addressing the method-sensitivity problem that arises when any single test is taken in isolation.
Recent work on causal method reliability reinforces this multi-method rationale.
\citet{ruiz2026causalaudit} propose Causal-Audit, a pre-screening framework that validates causal assumptions before method selection and achieves 62\% false positive reduction; whereas their approach filters methods \emph{ex ante}, our consensus framework validates conclusions \emph{ex post} across methods already applied.
\citet{yi2026causalcompass} benchmark causal discovery robustness under eight misspecification scenarios and confirm that no single method dominates universally, directly supporting the multi-method rationale of our consensus framework.
Independently, \citet{sahoo2026calibration} show that calibration metrics are sensitive to training-distribution perturbation beyond the iterative collapse setting, suggesting that ECE-based canary signals may be confounded by non-collapse sources of calibration drift.
\citet{falahati2026curated} prove that pluralistic curation of synthetic data can prevent iterative collapse entirely, implying that canary detection is most relevant in uncontrolled data pipelines where such curation is absent.

\paragraph{Analytical robustness in ML research.}

The broader issue of researcher degrees of freedom in ML has received increasing attention.
\citet{bell2022modeling} introduced multiverse analysis to machine learning, where pipeline choices create a combinatorial space of possible results; \citet{coretta2023multidimensional} provided direct evidence through a many-analysts design in which 46 independent teams analyzed identical data and reached substantially different conclusions; and \citet{kapoor2024reforms} synthesized these concerns into REFORMS, a 32-item consensus checklist for ML-based science.
Our work applies this multiverse perspective to model collapse: five statistical methods across six contamination regimes produce conclusions that range from universal significance to complete null on the same dataset.

Table~\ref{tab:method-comparison} summarizes the methodological coverage of existing canary and monitoring analyses across the diagnostic dimensions identified in \S\ref{sec:pitfalls}.
No prior work combines all six dimensions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Methodological comparison of canary and monitoring analyses in the model collapse literature. \checkmark\ = present, $\times$ = absent, $\circ$ = partial (${\leq}2$ levels or limited replication). Diff.\ = differencing or stationarity controls for spurious regression. Multi-M.\ = cross-validation across ${\geq}2$ independent statistical methods. MTC = multiple testing correction (e.g., Bonferroni, BH-FDR). Regime = systematic variation of contamination level~$\alpha$. Seeds = ${\geq}3$ independent random seeds. Arch.\ = validation on ${\geq}2$ architecturally distinct model families.}
\label{tab:method-comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccccccl}
\toprule
Work & Diff. & Multi-M. & MTC & Regime & Seeds & Arch. & Metrics \\
\midrule
\citet{shumailov2024curse}     & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\circ$    & \checkmark & \checkmark & PPL \\
\citet{du2025scales}           & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $\times$   & ECE, Acc, Dist-$n$ \\
\citet{gambetta2024surplexity} & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & Surplexity, Ent \\
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & Spectral \\
DCES~\cite{dces2026counter}    & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & ECE, Ent, PPL \\
\midrule
\textbf{Ours}                  & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & Ent, ECE, PPL, Dist-$n$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

In summary, the model collapse literature has established the phenomenon and proposed monitoring metrics, while the econometric literature provides the statistical tools for temporal precedence testing.
However, no prior work bridges these two bodies of literature with the methodological rigor that short, non-stationary time series demand: systematic multi-method cross-validation, differencing diagnostics, false discovery correction, and regime-dependent calibration.
Our consensus framework fills this gap.
